newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Toyota sees 7 pct rise in non-Japan output.
newsitem.headline: Toyota sees 7 pct rise in non-Japan output.

text.p: Toyota Motor Co Chairman Shoichiro Toyoda on Friday said the company aimed to increase production outside Japan this year by more than seven percent.

Speaking to journalists at the inauguration of a plant near Buenos Aires, where Toyota makes Hilux pickup trucks, he said the company wanted to boost output to 1.45 million vehicles this year from 1.35 million in 1996.
He also affirmed the company's plans to double output in Britain to 200,000 vehicles a year.

Asked by Reuters whether that goal entailed the building of a new British plant, Toyoda said the company intended to upgrade the existing facility. He declined to specify the size of any investment, saying with a smile that it would be "the lowest possible."
Toyoda said the company was still considering whether to build a new European plant.
He also affirmed that Toyota was weighing plans to list shares on the New York Stock Exchange but offered no details.
Referring to the company's decision to invest $150 million in Argentina, he said that reflected Toyota's "globalization philosophy: to make products where the market is."

The plant in Zarate, 50 miles (80 km) north of Buenos Aires, will make 10,000 units of the 4x4 and 4x2 single- and double-cabin Hiluxes in 1997. Production is scheduled to double next year. The plant employs 500 workers, and the payroll is expected to increase to 850 at a later stage.

Half of the output is earmarked for the domestic market and half for Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, the country's partners in the Mercosur customs union. The Mercosur countries have a total population of more than 200 million.
Toyota aims to capture a 10 percent share of the Mercosur automobile market by 2000 with estimated sales of 300,000 vehicles in South America. It also has plants in Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela.
"Output and sales are two wheels on a single axis," Toyoda said.

He said reforms launched by Argentine President Carlos Menem -- who attended the plant opening -- laid the foundations for political and economic stability that prompted the company to choose Argentina for the new facility.

As Toyoda was speaking in Argentina, the company reported in Tokyo that its Japanese output in February fell 13.5 percent year-on-year because of a fire disrupted its parts supply. The incident caused exports to fall year-on-year for the first time in two months.
Still, Toyota's sales in Japan rose for the sixth month in a row, reflecting persistent strong demand for new recreational vehicles.
In December, Toyota started building another plant in Brazil, where it will make its flagship Corolla sedan beginning in 1998. More than 20 million Corollas have been sold since 1969.
